video.title: The Simplest $7M Business You've Never Heard Of

summary: Michael Clark describes how he and his wife built The Flower Letters, a business that sends serialized stories and illustrated extras by post. They started with Instagram and Facebook ads, built an email list, and now sell multiple stories through monthly and prepaid subscriptions, gift products, and some retail placement. Clark credits prepaid plans, repeat and gift buyers, and continued investment in marketing and new stories, while describing high manual fulfillment needs and seasonal peaks. The host also explores other postal subscription ideas and shares his wife’s planned recipe-by-mail club.

speakers.name: Michael Clark
speakers.description: Co-founder and CEO of The Flower Letters.

ideas.name: The Flower Letters
ideas.one_liner: A mailed subscription that delivers an illustrated, serialized story in letters and themed inserts.
ideas.business_model: Monthly or prepaid annual subscriptions, with one-off sales of tins and other add-ons.
ideas.customer: Primarily women aged 35 and older, including people buying a sentimental gift for a mother, sister, friend, or themselves.
ideas.problem: Customers want a distinctive, giftable experience and something enjoyable to look forward to; buyers also want stories and gifts that feel personal.
ideas.offer: Two sequential story letters a month for a year, with artwork and varying inserts such as postcards, bookmarks, and era-related items. Customers can choose from several story subscriptions, mostly historical fiction, plus fantasy.

pricing.model: Monthly subscription or prepaid annual story; one-off add-ons and shipping may be charged separately.

price_points.label: Shipping when charged; free shipping is used in some promotions

pricing.notes: Clark says the annual prepaid option is attractive to customers and reduces reliance on conventional month-to-month subscription billing. The transcript mentions other possible add-ons, but gives no prices for them.

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook and Instagram ads became the main acquisition channel. They started testing ads with small spends after launching; an early marketing collaborator later ran the ads. Clark says the current acquisition cost is much higher than in the early days.

quote.text: So early on we started trying to acquire email addresses and so we can connect with people that way.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

acquisition_channels.details: The founders created a Flower Letters Instagram account and posted the product. Clark says the company initially got sign-ups after putting the offer out; his wife had previously sold paintings through her own Instagram.

quote.text: No, we just we started a flower letters Instagram, put it out.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

acquisition_channels.details: Clark says customers refer friends and that a loyal customer base is excited to try new stories.

quote.text: A lot of people referred this to their friends.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

acquisition_channels.details: The website asks visitors for an email address in exchange for a discount. The email list is used for campaigns, including win-back campaigns for previous customers.

quote.text: That's the first sort of on-site funnel is you ask for their email address for a discount.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: The company has a product in the Newport Mansions gift shops. Clark describes Costco placement as an aspiration, not a confirmed channel.

quote.text: One of their the person that runs their gift shop signed up, reached out like, "What if you wrote a story about the Gilded Age and we could put it in our shops?" We were like, "Yeah, that's totally cool."
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

ideas.delivery: Hanny writes the stories and creates the art and inserts; Clark handles the business. A team in a Utah warehouse handles each item and stuffs the letters by hand before mailing them. They built a redemption website for retail gift purchases where buyers scan a QR code and enter an address.
unit_economics_claims: Monthly price is $12; prepaid annual price is $100.
Materials and postage-related contents cost about $2 to $3 at their volume, according to Clark.
Early customer acquisition cost was roughly $15 to $20; Clark says it later rose to $40 to $50.
Clark reports annual churn of about 5% and lifetime value of about $180 across 12 months.
Clark says email drives 38% to 50% of revenue at times.
The company spent $2.6 million on Meta advertising last year, according to Clark.
tools: Retail redemption website and QR codes
Unnamed subscription software for monthly billing
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated as a specific amount; the host describes the initial launch as having almost no money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated precisely. The first letters were sent at the end of August; the host says the business reached about $36,000 in monthly recurring revenue within its first four months.

acquisition.how: Paid social campaigns, website email capture, and email win-back campaigns can be run with agents and routine human review. Creative, audience choices, ad spend, and UK-compliant email consent still need oversight.

onboarding.how: A website can collect orders and addresses, and the retail redemption flow uses a QR code and web form. Exceptions and gift recipient details may need human help.

delivery.how: Writing and illustrating the stories are creative work, and staff handle and hand-stuff physical letters. Agents can assist with planning or operational analysis but cannot perform the core physical fulfillment.

billing.how: Online monthly billing can use subscription software, but Clark says annual prepaid subscriptions are handled through their own process rather than subscription software.

support.how: Agents could answer routine order questions, but the company promises to make problems right and Clark describes calling upset customers, so sensitive cases need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: A serialized postal gift subscription can work in the UK. The business would need UK postage and fulfillment economics, applicable VAT and consumer rules, and UK-specific seasonal planning. Email acquisition should use appropriate consent or another valid UK basis; the transcript's Utah warehouse and US ad costs do not transfer directly.

risks: Every letter must arrive in the right order for the story to work; missed or confusing contents can undermine the promise.
Writing a complete serialized story is harder to produce and operate than a standalone monthly letter.
The business has sharp seasonal peaks, especially around Mother's Day, and needs enough fulfillment capacity and staffing.
Meta ad costs have risen substantially from the early acquisition costs Clark reports.
Physical fulfillment remains labor-intensive and exposed to postage, supply, and staffing constraints.
An insert was removed after the team learned that customers found it offensive.
Gift recipients may dislike the product, prompting the purchaser to cancel.
Reliance on paid Meta acquisition creates platform and margin risk; Clark says email is important as an owned audience.

tactics.name: Validate with real customers, not only friends and family
steps: Put the offer in front of people outside the founders' immediate family and friends.
Use sign-ups and purchases from people who fit the target market as evidence of interest.
Avoid treating supportive family purchases as proof that the product has found its customer.

quote.text: If you're launching a product or service, don't tell your family and friends. They'll give you a false positive.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Start with a small paid-social test
steps: Launch the product page and initial social presence.
Test Facebook and Instagram ads with small spends.
Track customer acquisition cost and bring in someone with advertising skills when the early tests show promise.

quote.text: October, we started dabbling in ads, just spending a few bucks here and there and people started showing up.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Capture email addresses from paid traffic
steps: Send website visitors to an on-site email form.
Offer a discount in exchange for an email address.
Use the list for customer communication and win-back campaigns, and treat consent and UK direct-marketing rules as part of the setup.

quote.text: That's the first sort of on-site funnel is you ask for their email address for a discount.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Make prepaid annual plans attractive
steps: Offer a prepaid annual story alongside monthly billing.
Set the annual price so buyers see a lower monthly equivalent.
Use the prepaid option to fund fulfillment earlier and reduce cancellations during the story.

quote.text: The key to our growth has been the prepaid option like a year up front.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Expand the story catalogue to serve existing customers
steps: Develop additional stories for customers who already enjoy the product.
Give a customer options to choose another story rather than relying only on one story renewing.
Use email to tell previous buyers when a new story is available.

quote.text: That has been our key to our growth and success is adding more stories, being able to kind of service a customer as they are, any story they would like
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Use win-back campaigns for completed or inactive customers
steps: Identify customers who may not know about a new story.
Send them an email campaign about the new option.
Measure repeat purchases across stories rather than treating each story as a simple auto-renewal.

quote.text: So we'll we'll have win back campaigns where people maybe haven't, you know, been paying attention, know we have another story, so we'll do email campaigns to try to win them back.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Build fulfillment capacity around seasonal peaks
steps: Plan staffing and inventory ahead of Mother's Day and Christmas.
Use free shipping in busy promotional periods to reduce barriers to entry, then charge shipping at other times.
Check staffing availability during Christmas, when employees may want to be with family.

quote.text: So you have these big peaks in Mother's Day and you have to figure out okay we've got to make sure we've got enough operations to go then to get to the next one
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Improve hand-fulfillment productivity
steps: Have an operations manager examine how letters are prepared and stuffed.
Improve the process before adding more staff.
Track both staffing and monthly volume to see whether operational changes increase output.

quote.text: We used to have like 15 people stuffing 20,000 letters. Now we have five doing 120,000 a month.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Make gift products easy to redeem
steps: Sell a physical giftable product through a retail location.
Add a QR code that takes the recipient to a redemption website.
Collect the recipient's delivery address through the site.

quote.text: So we built out a whole redemption website and you know where you can come in, you scan a QR code, pulls up, you enter your address and you're good to go.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Use customer feedback to correct product problems
steps: Monitor customer questions about whether an order is complete.
Check what was included in each mailing and clarify differences between installments.
Remove or change inserts when customers flag a problem.

quote.text: there was one where we had to do something because people kept reaching out. I was like, did I get everything?
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Test a market with a concept page and email sign-up
steps: Define a product concept and build a simple website describing it.
Add a coming-soon form to collect email addresses.
Run small ad tests and assess whether enough of the target market opts in before investing heavily.

quote.text: I would develop a product a concept idea and I would build a website. I would put up a a form coming soon.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Start product research with a customer of one
steps: Start with a specific person whose preferences you understand, such as yourself.
Avoid adding a feature just because it sounds useful.
If a proposed feature is a large lift, wait or test it before committing to ongoing production.

quote.text: If you don't really know how to figure that out, just start with a customer of one. You, right?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Pair creative work with commercial ownership
steps: Assign a clear owner to the creative product and a clear owner to business operations.
Make sure the person creating the work is supported by someone focused on marketing, customer acquisition, and unit economics.
Protect the creative quality that makes the product distinctive.

quote.text: She's the creator, right? And I think most people, and I think it's saw with Hannah, my wife's name's Hannah as well, but with with the person you had on your podcast, works well with us, is she can really focus on the creative and I can really focus on the business.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Use AI for business analysis while keeping the core creative work human
steps: Use AI to summarize customer email patterns and analyze advertising data.
Feed in financials for business analysis and decision support.
Keep human authors responsible for the story and evaluate AI-generated entertainment carefully.

quote.text: I use it every day to process thought. I'll, you know, do analysis on a string of emails I've received, pull in data from our Facebook ads and have it run an analysis on our efficiency
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Treat a serialized story as a more demanding product than standalone mail
steps: Choose a standalone monthly letter if the goal is a simpler product to create and fulfill.
If using a continuing story, write and plan the sequence so each installment connects and arrives in order.
Account for the greater creative and operational workload before launching.

quote.text: Know and but also know what you're signing up for. Um, if you're doing a story, it's much harder than doing a standalone monthto month
quote.speaker: Michael Clark
